questions.question: Foundation Name the four magnetic elements.

points.text: Q1: Iron, nickel, cobalt and steel (an alloy of iron).

questions.question: Foundation State the rule for what happens when two north poles are brought close together.

points.text: Q2: Like poles repel — two north poles will repel each other.

questions.question: Higher Explain the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.

points.text: Q3: A permanent magnet always produces its own magnetic field and always has north and south poles. An induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed in the field of a permanent magnet and loses its magnetism when removed from that field. Induced magnets are always attracted to the permanent magnet, while permanent magnets can attract or repel each other depending on which poles are facing.

questions.question: Foundation In which direction do magnetic field lines point?

points.text: Q4: Magnetic field lines point from north to south (outside the magnet).

questions.question: Higher Describe how you would use iron filings and a plotting compass to show the shape and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

points.text: Q5: To show the shape: sprinkle iron filings evenly around the magnet on a flat surface. The filings will align along the field lines, showing the shape of the field. To show the direction: place a plotting compass near the north pole of the magnet. The compass needle points along the field line (its north-seeking end points from N to S). markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and draw around it, marking the north and south poles. Place a small plotting compass near the north pole of the magnet. The compass needle aligns with the field line at that point. Mark the two ends of the needle with dots on the paper. Move the compass so that the tail end of the needle is at the position where the head was previously marked. Mark the new head position. Repeat this process, moving the compass along the field line, until you reach the south pole. Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow pointing from north to south. Repeat from different starting points near the north pole to map several field lines. The field lines show the direction of the magnetic field — arrows point from north to south, showing the direction a free north pole would move. The strength of the field is shown by the spacing of the lines — where lines are closer together (near the poles), the field is stronger; where they are further apart, the field is weaker. Mark scheme: 1 mark — place magnet on paper and draw around it, 1 mark — use compass to mark needle positions and move along the field line, 1 mark — join dots and add arrow from N to S, 1 mark — repeat from different starting points for several lines, 1 mark — direction shown by arrows (N to S), 1 mark — strength shown by line spacing (closer = stronger)
